item.title: PDF Search Program: Exploring PageIndex, Streamlit, and Page Links
item.description:
"Warranty period - 18 months." A nice answer. But what if the contract says 12? Or the number 18 is in the storage section, and the model just latched onto it? In a chat, such errors hide behind a smooth phrase. I wanted a different path: ask a question to a PDF, get an answer, and with one click, open the physical page of the source file that the model refers to. Thus, PDF Desk was born – a small application on Python, Streamlit, PageIndex, and PDFium. One active document. No user database. The index and the source PDF remain on your computer; when using an external model, the document's text still goes to its provider. Next – where is the boundary between SDK and application. Why a bare `/models` is not enough to check the connection. What makes up the index identifier. And why a link to an existing page doesn't yet mean the answer is proven. At the end, a live run of DeepSeek, including the browser, and scenarios for which this run is insufficient. Read more

item.title: Cheap, but Not Accurate: Analyzing the LLM Agent Memory Trust Controller
item.description:
In 2024, the New York City Hall launched the MyCity chatbot, a digital assistant for small business owners. It was intended to be a convenient guide to city rules and laws. However, the bot gave advice that could have led to fines and lawsuits for entrepreneurs, such as not paying employees their full tips or firing someone for complaining about harassment. The correct information was available in the bot's own knowledge base alongside outdated information. It turned out the bot simply couldn't distinguish between correct and incorrect information when both were readily available. Read more

item.title: Which LLM to choose: building our own benchmark
item.description:
Usually, when choosing an LLM, people first look at ratings. The problem with ratings is that they don't tell you how a model will handle your tasks and how much it will cost. In our lab, we use an electronic lab notebook – a database where data from all experiments and measurements are recorded, and an AI assistant answers questions based on it. Naturally, the question arose: which model should power this assistant? Public ratings didn't provide an answer, so we created our own benchmark: twenty-four questions related to our work, run on the live journal through mcp on DeepSeek, ChatGPT, and Claude models. Next, I'll show you how we collected these twenty-four questions, what results we got from nineteen combinations of models and reasoning effort levels in about 450 runs, and how to create a similar test for your own tasks. Read more

item.title: MTPLX vs. oMLX: One Model, Two Servers, a 3-6x Difference
item.description:
Part two. Part one was "Local Code Agent on Mac: MTPLX + pi + Qwen3.8-27B". In the first part, I ran the pi code agent on a local Qwen3.8-27B via MTPLX and tackled a complex task in different reasoning modes. A doubt remained, which MTPLX itself couldn't resolve: how much of this was due to its multi-token prediction (MTP), and how much would have worked with any MLX wrapper? A conversation with ChatGPT was the catalyst. I asked which MLX server to use on a MacBook Pro with M4 Max and received a confident answer: oMLX is faster and higher quality than others on such hardware. It sounded plausible, and I was doubly interested in checking. I installed oMLX, took the same model and the same task, and repeated all the same modes. I also answered questions from the comments on the first part – about the default mode, fan noise, and memory. The short conclusion: the advice was not confirmed. In my runs, MTPLX finished the task 2.8–6.4 times faster, and in hidden tests, the combinations were equal. The caveats are also short: the model builds are different, and I ran each mode on oMLX only once. Read on.

item.title: Negotiations are not just about work: how I teach AI not to give in

item.title: AI has knowledge, humans have context
item.description:
Text increasingly reaches the reader through two AIs: one the author writes with, and one that summarizes for the reader. In instrumentation and control, this is called a measurement channel, and it has an unpleasant property: errors accumulate. Knowledge passes through such a channel well, context does not. I analyze what context is lost, why a model error common to all its readers is more dangerous than ordinary misunderstanding, and how to verify the channel from both sides—using my own comment that went into the negative as an example. Read on

item.title: In Joy and Sorrow, or How Neural Networks Understand User Emotions
item.description:
Remember the saddest short story? Today it might look like this: 'I was laid off,' a person wrote to Claude. 'It seems you're scared about the future,' replied the AI. In a survey of 500 people, 17.2% reported turning to ChatGPT for mental health support. And indeed, models seem to articulate feelings quite well. item.title: Forecasting infection outbreaks
item.description:
I've built an MVP of a decision support system for epidemiological monitoring. The goal was technical: to test the full path from a time series per territory to risk calculation and output in a conversational interface. An important limitation: the epidemiological dynamics in this MVP are synthetic. The names of municipalities, area, population, density, and temperature from Yandex Weather were real. Vaccination rates, number of cases, incidence, and the target label were generated programmatically. Therefore, the presented metrics say nothing about the model's ability to predict real ARVI outbreaks. On such data, it's impossible to conclude that one architecture is better than another: the model primarily learns the patterns embedded in the synthetic series generator. Nevertheless, the setup proved useful. It allowed testing the construction of time windows, chronological splitting, normalization, training, inference, notification thresholds, and handling of a rare positive class. Read more
